items.title: 10.1 An Overview
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

Zeno argued that you can never walk across a room: first you must cover half the distance, then half of what remains, then half of that, and so on, with infinitely many steps. Yet the sum \(\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\cdots\) of those step lengths seems to be \(1\), the width of the room. Can an endless list of positive numbers have a finite total? What would “total” even mean for infinitely many terms? The answer in this chapter is to stop adding forever and to look instead at a list of running totals and where it is heading. That turns the question about an infinite sum into a question about a sequence, so we begin with sequences.

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • write out terms of a sequence given by an explicit formula or by a recurrence, and find a formula that fits a pattern (and say why a pattern never proves a formula);

  • recognise arithmetic and geometric sequences and use their closed forms;

  • estimate the limit of a sequence from a table or a graph, and explain why such an estimate is evidence and not proof;

  • define the partial sums of a series and use them to decide, in simple cases, what a series adds up to;

  • recover the terms of a series from its partial sums, and use the finite geometric sum formula;

  • write a short induction proof.

items.title: Sequences: lists of numbers
items.text:
Definition 10.1.1: Sequence

A sequence is an ordered list of real numbers

\[a_1,\ a_2,\ a_3,\ \dots,\ a_n,\ \dots\]

with one number \(a_n\) (the \(n\)th term) for each positive integer \(n\). We write the sequence as \(\{a_n\}\), or \(\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) when we want to show where it starts. Equivalently, a sequence is a function whose inputs are the positive integers: \(n\mapsto a_n\). Sometimes it is convenient to start at \(n=0\) or at another integer.

Definition 10.1.2: Explicit and recursive definitions

A sequence is defined explicitly when a formula gives \(a_n\) directly from \(n\), for example \(a_n=n^2\). It is defined recursively (or by a recurrence) when the first term or terms are given and a rule gives each later term from the ones before it, for example \(a_1=1\) and \(a_{n+1}=2a_n+1\).

An explicit formula lets you jump straight to the thousandth term. A recurrence makes you walk there one step at a time, but it is often the more natural description: “each year the balance grows by \(3\%\)” is a recurrence long before it is a formula.

Example 10.1.3: Terms from an explicit formula

List the first five terms of \(a_n=\dfrac{2n-1}{n+2}\).

Solution. Substitute \(n=1,2,3,4,5\):

\[a_1=\frac13,\quad a_2=\frac34,\quad a_3=\frac55=1,\quad a_4=\frac76,\quad a_5=\frac97 .\]

Notice that the terms seem to creep upward without passing \(2\); the numerator is nearly twice the denominator when \(n\) is large. We return to this kind of question below.

Example 10.1.4: Terms from a recurrence

A sequence has \(a_1=2\) and \(a_{n+1}=3a_n-1\). List the first five terms.

Solution. The rule says: to get the next term, triple the current one and subtract \(1\). Starting from \(a_1=2\):

\[a_2=3(2)-1=5,\quad a_3=3(5)-1=14,\quad a_4=3(14)-1=41,\quad a_5=3(41)-1=122 .\]

Each term uses the one just before it, so we cannot find \(a_5\) without computing \(a_2\), \(a_3\) and \(a_4\) first. A recurrence is useless without its starting value: with \(a_1=0\) the same rule gives \(-1,-4,-13,\dots\)

Example 10.1.5: A recurrence that uses two earlier terms

Let \(a_1=1\), \(a_2=3\) and \(a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n\). List the first six terms.

Solution. Two starting values are needed because each term uses the previous two:

\[a_3=3+1=4,\quad a_4=4+3=7,\quad a_5=7+4=11,\quad a_6=11+7=18 .\]

With starting values \(1,1\) the same rule produces the Fibonacci numbers \(1,1,2,3,5,8,\dots\)

items.title: Finding a formula from a pattern
items.text:
Given a few terms, we often want a rule that produces them. This is guesswork informed by experience: look for a common difference, a common ratio, squares, factorials, alternating signs.

Example 10.1.6: Four patterns

Find an explicit formula \(a_n\) (\(n=1,2,3,\dots\)) that fits each list.

(a) \(5,\ 8,\ 11,\ 14,\ 17,\dots\) (b) \(3,\ 6,\ 12,\ 24,\dots\) (c) \(\frac12,\ -\frac14,\ \frac18,\ -\frac1{16},\dots\) (d) \(2,\ 6,\ 12,\ 20,\ 30,\dots\)

Solution. (a) Each term is \(3\) more than the one before, so \(a_n=5+3(n-1)=3n+2\). (b) Each term is twice the one before, starting at \(3\): \(a_n=3\cdot2^{n-1}\). (c) The denominators are \(2^n\) and the signs alternate, starting positive at \(n=1\): \(a_n=\dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2^n}\). (d) The differences \(4,6,8,10\) increase by \(2\) each time, which suggests a quadratic; comparing with \(n^2\) (\(1,4,9,16,25\)) shows each term is \(n\) more than \(n^2\), so \(a_n=n^2+n=n(n+1)\). Always substitute \(n=1,2,3,\dots\) back into your formula to check that it reproduces the list.

Pause and think 10.1.1: Does a list determine a sequence?

The list \(1,2,4,8,16,\dots\) looks like \(a_n=2^{n-1}\). The number of regions into which \(n\) points on a circle, joined in all possible ways, cut the disk is \(1,2,4,8,16\) for \(n=1,\dots,5\). What do you predict for \(n=6\)? Then check the formula \(r_n=\dfrac{n^4-6n^3+23n^2-18n+24}{24}\) at \(n=1,\dots,6\). What does this say about guessing a formula from a finite list?

Answer and discussion

The doubling pattern predicts \(32\) for \(n=6\). The formula gives \(1,2,4,8,16\) at \(n=1,\dots,5\), and at \(n=6\) it gives \(\frac{744}{24}=31\) (the numerator is \(1296-1296+828-108+24\)). So two different rules agree on five terms and disagree on the sixth: finitely many terms never determine a sequence. A pattern is a conjecture to be proved, for instance by induction, as in Example 10.1.22.

items.title: Arithmetic and geometric sequences
items.text:
Definition 10.1.7: Arithmetic and geometric sequences

A sequence is arithmetic if \(a_{n+1}=a_n+d\) for a constant common difference \(d\), and geometric if \(a_{n+1}=r\,a_n\) for a constant common ratio \(r\).

Theorem 10.1.8: Closed forms

(a) If \(a_{n+1}=a_n+d\) for all \(n\ge1\), then \(a_n=a_1+(n-1)d\) for all \(n\ge1\).

(b) If \(a_{n+1}=r\,a_n\) for all \(n\ge1\), then \(a_n=a_1\,r^{\,n-1}\) for all \(n\ge1\).

Proof. Both are proved by induction on \(n\).

(a) Base case. For \(n=1\) the formula says \(a_1=a_1+0\cdot d\), which is true. Inductive step. Suppose \(a_n=a_1+(n-1)d\) for some \(n\ge1\). Then

\[a_{n+1}=a_n+d=a_1+(n-1)d+d=a_1+n\,d=a_1+\big((n+1)-1\big)d,\]

which is the formula for \(n+1\). By induction the formula holds for every \(n\ge1\).

(b) Base case. For \(n=1\) the formula says \(a_1=a_1r^0\), which is true. Inductive step. Suppose \(a_n=a_1r^{n-1}\). Then \(a_{n+1}=r\,a_n=r\cdot a_1r^{n-1}=a_1r^{n}=a_1r^{(n+1)-1}\), which is the formula for \(n+1\). By induction it holds for every \(n\ge1\). ◻ ∎

Example 10.1.9: Using the closed forms

(a) An arithmetic sequence has \(a_1=7\) and \(d=-4\). Find \(a_{20}\). (b) A geometric sequence has \(a_1=5\) and \(r=\frac12\). Find \(a_8\). (c) A geometric sequence has \(a_4=24\) and \(a_7=192\). Find \(a_1\) and \(r\).

Solution. (a) By Theorem 10.1.8(a), \(a_{20}=7+19(-4)=-69\). (b) By part (b) of the theorem, \(a_8=5\left(\frac12\right)^7=\frac5{128}\). (c) Write the two given terms with the closed form: \(a_4=a_1r^3=24\) and \(a_7=a_1r^6=192\). Dividing the second equation by the first, \(r^3=8\), so \(r=2\) (the real cube root). Then \(a_1=24/2^3=3\). Check: \(3\cdot2^6=192\).

Knowledge Check 10.1.1: Terms and formulas

(a) A sequence has \(b_1=4\) and \(b_{n+1}=2b_n-3\). List \(b_1,\dots,b_4\). (b) Find a formula for \(10,7,4,1,\dots\) (c) A geometric sequence has \(a_1=64\) and \(r=\frac12\). Find \(a_7\).

items.title: Limits of sequences: what happens for large \(n\)?
items.text:
The question that drives this chapter is about the long run: as \(n\) grows, do the terms settle down to a single number?

Definition 10.1.10: Limit of a sequence (informal)

If the terms \(a_n\) get and stay as close as we like to a number \(L\) once \(n\) is large enough, we say the sequence converges to \(L\) and write \(\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=L\). A sequence that does not converge to any number diverges. The precise version, with \(\varepsilon\) and \(N\), is Definition A.2 in the appendix and is the basis of Section 10.2.

Example 10.1.11: Estimating a limit from a table

Estimate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{3n+1}{n+4}\).

Solution. Compute some terms: \(a_{10}=\frac{31}{14}\approx2.2143\), \(a_{100}=\frac{301}{104}\approx2.8942\), \(a_{1000}=\frac{3001}{1004}\approx2.9890\). The terms increase toward \(3\). That is no accident: for large \(n\) the \(+1\) and the \(+4\) hardly matter, and the ratio is close to \(\frac{3n}{n}=3\). We estimate that the limit is \(3\). This is evidence, not proof; Section 10.2 shows how to prove it with limit laws.

Example 10.1.12: A famous limit

Estimate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\dfrac1n\right)^n\).

Solution. The base tends to \(1\) and the exponent tends to infinity, so it is not clear what happens. Tabulate: \(a_1=2\), \(a_{10}\approx2.5937\), \(a_{100}\approx2.7048\), \(a_{1000}\approx2.7169\), \(a_{10^6}\approx2.71828\). The terms increase and appear to level off near \(2.718\ldots\), the number \(e\). The limit is indeed \(e\); proving that needs more than a table (a bounded, increasing sequence converges, by the Monotone Convergence Theorem A.5 of the appendix, but identifying the limit as \(e\) comes with the calculus of logarithms). Notice what the table does not tell us: neither factor alone, \(1+\frac1n\to1\) or exponent \(\to\infty\), gives the answer. The two effects compete and the compromise is \(e\).

A table is not a proof

A table can suggest a limit and can never prove one. Terms that agree with a number to six decimal places for \(n\le10^6\) may still wander off later (Pause and think 10.1.2). Treat tables and graphs as a way to form a conjecture and to catch errors, and use limit laws, the Squeeze Theorem and the theory of Section 10.2 to prove it.

Knowledge Check 10.1.2: Estimating limits

(a) Compute \(a_{10}\), \(a_{100}\) and \(a_{1000}\) for \(a_n=\dfrac{4n-1}{n+5}\) and estimate the limit. (b) Why can the estimate in part (a) not be called a proof? (c) Decide, by looking at the even- and odd-numbered terms, whether \(c_n=(-1)^n\dfrac{n}{n+1}\) converges.

Pause and think 10.1.2: How far can a table be trusted?

Suppose \(a_n=5+\dfrac{n}{10^{10}}\). Compute \(a_n\) for \(n=10,\ 10^3\) and \(10^6\) and describe what a table of those values suggests. What does the sequence actually do as \(n\to\infty\)?

Answer and discussion

\(a_{10}=5.000000001\), \(a_{1000}=5.0000001\) and \(a_{10^6}=5.0001\). A table of these values suggests the limit \(5\). But \(a_n=5+\frac n{10^{10}}\) grows without bound: once \(n>10^{11}\) the term exceeds \(15\). So the sequence diverges, and a table that stops at \(10^6\) cannot see it.

items.title: Infinite series and partial sums
items.text:
Definition 10.1.13: Series and partial sums

Given a sequence \(\{a_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\), the infinite series \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_k=a_1+a_2+a_3+\cdots\) is the formal sum of all its terms. Its \(n\)th partial sum is the sum of the first \(n\) terms,

\[S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_k=a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n .\]

The numbers \(S_1,S_2,S_3,\dots\) form the sequence of partial sums \(\{S_n\}\). If \(S_n o S\) we say the series converges, call \(S\) its sum and write \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k=S\); otherwise the series diverges.

This is exactly how the guiding question gets answered: “what is an infinite sum?” means “what is the limit of the finite sums?”. Section 10.3 makes this the official definition and develops it; here we explore with simple cases.

Theorem 10.1.14: Terms and partial sums

Let \(S_n=a_1+\cdots+a_n\) be the partial sums of the series \(\sum a_k\). Then \(a_1=S_1\) and \(a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\) for \(n\ge2\). If every \(a_k>0\), then \(S_1<S_2<S_3<\cdots\), that is, the partial sums are increasing.

Proof. \(S_1=a_1\) by definition. For \(n\ge2\),

\[S_n-S_{n-1}=(a_1+\cdots+a_{n-1}+a_n)-(a_1+\cdots+a_{n-1})=a_n .\]

If all \(a_k>0\), then \(S_n-S_{n-1}=a_n>0\), so \(S_n>S_{n-1}\) for every \(n\ge2\). ◻ ∎

Theorem 10.1.15: Finite geometric sum

For every real number \(r e1\) and every integer \(n\ge1\),

\[1+r+r^2+\cdots+r^{n-1}= rac{1-r^n}{1-r}.\]

Proof. Let \(G=1+r+\cdots+r^{n-1}\). Multiply by \(1-r\) and let the terms cancel in pairs:

\[(1-r)G=(1+r+\cdots+r^{n-1})-(r+r^2+\cdots+r^{n})=1-r^n ,\]

because every power \(r^1,\dots,r^{n-1}\) appears once with each sign. Since \(r e1\) we may divide by \(1-r\). ◻ ∎

Consequently the partial sums of the geometric series \(\sum_{k=1}^n a r^{k-1}\) are \(S_n=a\,\dfrac{1-r^n}{1-r}\) when \(r e1\).

Example 10.1.16: Zeno’s series

Find the partial sums of \( rac12+ rac14+ rac18+\cdots=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left( rac12 ight)^k\) and decide what the series adds up to.

Solution. The first partial sums are \(S_1= rac12\), \(S_2= rac34\), \(S_3= rac78\): each time we fill half of the remaining gap to \(1\). This suggests \(S_n=1- rac1{2^n}\). To prove it, use the finite geometric sum with first term \(a= rac12\) and ratio \(r= rac12\):

\[S_n= rac12\cdot rac{1-(1/2)^n}{1-1/2}=1- rac1{2^n}.\]

As \(n o\infty\), \( rac1{2^n} o0\), so \(S_n o1\) and the series converges to \(1\), in agreement with Zeno’s room.

Example 10.1.17: A telescoping series

Find a formula for \(S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac1{k(k+1)}\) and the sum of the series.

Solution. The key is the partial fraction identity \(\dfrac1{k(k+1)}=\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+1}\), which holds because \(\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+1}=\dfrac{(k+1)-k}{k(k+1)}\). Then the sum collapses:

\[S_n=\left(1- rac12 ight)+\left( rac12- rac13 ight)+\cdots+\left( rac1n- rac1{n+1} ight)=1- rac1{n+1}= rac n{n+1}.\]

Every term except the first and the last cancels with a neighbour. Since \( rac n{n+1}=1- rac1{n+1} o1\), the series converges to \(1\).

Example 10.1.18: A repeating decimal as a series

Write \(0.333\ldots\) as a series and find its sum.

Solution. \(0.333\ldots= rac3{10}+ rac3{100}+ rac3{1000}+\cdots\), a geometric series with \(a= rac3{10}\) and \(r= rac1{10}\). By the finite geometric sum,

\[S_n= rac3{10}\cdot rac{1-10^{-n}}{1- rac1{10}}= rac{1-10^{-n}}{3}.\]

Since \(10^{-n} o0\), \(S_n o rac13\). So “\(0.333\ldots= rac13\)” is a true statement about the limit of the partial sums \(0.3,\ 0.33,\ 0.333,\dots\)

Example 10.1.19: From partial sums back to terms

A series has partial sums \(S_n=2n^2+n\). Find its terms \(a_n\) and decide whether the series converges.

Solution. By Theorem 10.1.14, \(a_1=S_1=3\) and, for \(n\ge2\),

\[a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=(2n^2+n)- ig(2(n-1)^2+(n-1) ig)=4n-1 .\]

The formula \(4n-1\) also gives \(a_1=3\), so it works for every \(n\ge1\): the series is \(3+7+11+15+\cdots\). The partial sums \(2n^2+n\) grow without bound, so the series diverges. Check: \(3+7+11=21=S_3=2(9)+3\).

Knowledge Check 10.1.3: Partial sums

(a) Use the finite geometric sum to find \(S_n\) for \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}3\left( rac14 ight)^{k-1}\) and compute \(S_3\) both from the formula and directly. (b) A series has \(S_n=n^2+2n\). Find \(a_n\). (c) Is the series \(1+2+3+\cdots\) (whose partial sums are \(S_n= rac{n(n+1)}2\)) convergent?

Pause and think 10.1.3: Is \(0.999\ldots\) equal to \(1\)?

Write \(0.999\ldots\) as a series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac9{10^k}\), find a formula for its partial sums, and say what the series equals. Then explain, in your own words, why this is not a contradiction of the feeling that \(0.999\ldots\) is “just below” \(1\).

Answer and discussion

The partial sums are \(S_n=9\left( rac1{10}+\cdots+ rac1{10^n} ight)= rac9{10}\cdot rac{1-10^{-n}}{1- rac1{10}}=1-10^{-n}\), and \(1-10^{-n} o1\), so the series equals \(1\). Each partial sum (\(0.9,\ 0.99,\ 0.999,\dots\)) is below \(1\), and that is the source of the feeling; but the series is not any partial sum. Its value is the limit of the partial sums, and the limit of numbers that creep up to \(1\), getting and staying as close to it as we like, is \(1\). Nothing sits strictly between \(0.999\ldots\) and \(1\).

items.title: Looking ahead
items.text: Everything in the rest of the chapter grows out of these two ideas. Section 10.2 develops the limit of a sequence rigorously, including a theorem that decides many questions at once: a bounded, increasing sequence converges (Theorem A.5). Since the partial sums of a series with positive terms are increasing (Theorem 10.1.14), the same theorem will say that such a series converges exactly when its partial sums stay bounded. Later sections build tests that decide convergence without finding a formula for \(S_n\), and Chapter 11 turns series into the road to power series: infinite sums of powers of \(x\) that represent functions.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  1. Explicit formulas (Examples 10.1.20–10.1.21): terms, and solving \(a_n=\) a given value.

  2. Recurrences (Examples 10.1.22–10.1.23): exact and numerical terms, and a first look at a limit.

  3. Formulas from patterns (Examples 10.1.24–10.1.25): quadratic, exponential and mixed patterns.

  4. Limits from tables and graphs (Examples 10.1.26–10.1.27): a convergent and a divergent sequence.

  5. Models (Examples 10.1.28–10.1.29): compound growth and a repeated drug dose.

  6. Partial sums (Examples 10.1.30–10.1.31): a telescoping and a geometric series.

  7. Proofs (Examples 10.1.32–10.1.33): induction proofs, one for a sum and one for a recurrence.

items.title: Group 1: Explicit formulas
items.text:
Example 10.1.20: Terms and a target value

For \(a_n=n^2-3n\), list \(a_1,\dots,a_5\) and find the \(n\) for which \(a_n=130\).

Solution. Substituting, \(a_1=-2\), \(a_2=-2\), \(a_3=0\), \(a_4=4\), \(a_5=10\); the sequence dips below zero at the start because \(3n\) beats \(n^2\) for \(n=1,2\). To solve \(n^2-3n=130\), move everything to one side: \(n^2-3n-130=0\), which factors as \((n-13)(n+10)=0\). The root \(n=-10\) is not a positive integer, so it is rejected, and \(n=13\). Check: \(13^2-39=169-39=130\).

Example 10.1.21: Alternating signs and factorials

List the first four terms of \(a_n=\dfrac{(-1)^n2^n}{n!}\) and say what happens to the size of the terms.

Solution. The factor \((-1)^n\) gives the sign: negative for odd \(n\), positive for even \(n\). The size is \(2^n/n!\). So

\[a_1=-\frac21=-2,\quad a_2=\frac42=2,\quad a_3=-\frac86=-\frac43,\quad a_4=\frac{16}{24}=\frac23 .\]

The size at first grows (from \(2\) to \(2\)) and then shrinks, because each step multiplies the size by \(\frac2{n+1}\): the ratio \(\frac{2^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{2^n/n!}=\frac{2}{n+1}\) is less than \(1\) once \(n\ge2\). For example \(\frac{2^6}{6!}=\frac{64}{720}=\frac4{45}\). The factorial eventually beats any power.

items.title: Group 2: Recurrences
items.text:
Example 10.1.22: A recurrence with a surprise

Let \(a_1=1\) and \(a_{n+1}=\dfrac{a_n}{1+a_n}\). Find \(a_2,a_3,a_4\) and guess a formula.

Solution. \(a_2=\dfrac{1}{1+1}=\dfrac12\). Then \(a_3=\dfrac{1/2}{1+1/2}=\dfrac{1/2}{3/2}=\dfrac13\) and \(a_4=\dfrac{1/3}{4/3}=\dfrac14\). The pattern suggests \(a_n=\dfrac1n\). This is only a guess from four terms (compare Pause and think 10.1.1); we can prove it by induction: if \(a_n=\frac1n\) then \(a_{n+1}=\dfrac{1/n}{1+1/n}=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\). The guess is therefore correct.

Example 10.1.23: Repeated square roots

Let \(a_1=1\) and \(a_{n+1}=\sqrt{6+a_n}\). Compute \(a_2,a_3,a_4,a_5\) to four decimals and guess the limit.

Solution. Use a calculator at each step: \(a_2=\sqrt7\approx2.6458\), \(a_3=\sqrt{6+2.6458}\approx2.9404\), \(a_4\approx2.9900\), \(a_5\approx2.9983\). The terms increase and approach \(3\). A reason for the guess: if \(a_n\to L\) then also \(a_{n+1}\to L\), so \(L=\sqrt{6+L}\); squaring, \(L^2-L-6=0\), that is \((L-3)(L+2)=0\). Since all terms are positive, \(L=3\). (This argument assumes the limit exists; Section 10.2 shows when that is justified.)

items.title: Group 3: Formulas from patterns
items.text:
Example 10.1.24: A quadratic pattern

Find a formula for \(2,\ 5,\ 10,\ 17,\ 26,\dots\)

Solution. The differences are \(3,5,7,9\), increasing by \(2\) each time, so the pattern is quadratic with leading term \(n^2\). Comparing with \(1,4,9,16,25\), each term is exactly \(1\) larger: \(a_n=n^2+1\). Check: \(a_5=26\).

Example 10.1.25: Powers in the denominator and a shift

Find formulas for (a) \(\frac13,\ \frac29,\ \frac3{27},\ \frac4{81},\dots\) and (b) \(\frac32,\ \frac54,\ \frac98,\ \frac{17}{16},\dots\)

Solution. (a) Numerators \(1,2,3,4\) and denominators \(3,9,27,81=3^n\): \(a_n=\dfrac n{3^n}\). (b) The denominators are \(2^n\); the numerators \(3,5,9,17\) are \(2^n+1\) (that is, \(2+1,4+1,8+1,16+1\)). So \(b_n=\dfrac{2^n+1}{2^n}=1+\dfrac1{2^n}\), which also shows the terms decrease toward \(1\).

items.title: Group 4: Limits from tables and graphs
items.text:
Example 10.1.26: A convergent sequence from a table

Estimate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{5n}{2n+3}\).

Solution. \(a_{10}=\frac{50}{23}\approx2.1739\), \(a_{100}=\frac{500}{203}\approx2.4631\), \(a_{1000}=\frac{5000}{2003}\approx2.4963\). The terms increase toward \(2.5\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(n\) gives \(\dfrac{5}{2+3/n}\), and \(\frac3n\to0\), so the limit is \(\frac52\), which matches the table.

Example 10.1.27: A divergent sequence

Examine \(a_n=(-1)^n+\dfrac1n\) for large \(n\).

Solution. \(a_2=1.5\), \(a_3\approx-0.6667\), \(a_{100}=1.01\), \(a_{101}\approx-0.9901\). The even-numbered terms are near \(1\) and the odd-numbered terms are near \(-1\), so the terms do not settle down to one number: the sequence diverges. A graph shows two strings of dots, one hugging the line \(y=1\) and one hugging \(y=-1\). (If a limit \(L\) existed, all large terms would be near \(L\), and no number is within \(\frac12\) of both \(1\) and \(-1\); this is made precise in Appendix B.9.)

items.title: Group 5: Models
items.text:
Example 10.1.28: Compound growth

An account holds $2000 and earns \(3\%\) per year. Write the balance as a sequence and find when it first exceeds $3000.

Solution. Let \(A_n\) be the balance after \(n\) years. Each year the balance is multiplied by \(1.03\), so \(A_{n+1}=1.03A_n\) with \(A_0=2000\): a geometric sequence, \(A_n=2000(1.03)^n\). We need \(2000(1.03)^n>3000\), that is \((1.03)^n>1.5\). Trying values, \(A_{13}\approx2937.07<3000\) and \(A_{14}\approx3025.18>3000\). So the balance first exceeds $3000 after \(14\) years. (Taking logarithms, \(n>\ln1.5/\ln1.03\approx13.72\).)

Example 10.1.29: A repeated dose

A patient takes 100 mg of a drug each morning, and each day the body removes \(20\%\) of the drug present. Let \(D_n\) be the amount just after the \(n\)th dose. Find \(D_1,\dots,D_4\), and check that \(D_n=500(1-0.8^n)\) fits.

Solution. \(D_1=100\). Each day \(80\%\) remains, then \(100\) mg is added: \(D_{n+1}=0.8D_n+100\). So \(D_2=0.8(100)+100=180\), \(D_3=0.8(180)+100=244\), \(D_4=0.8(244)+100=295.2\). The formula gives \(500(1-0.8)=100\), \(500(1-0.64)=180\), \(500(1-0.512)=244\), \(500(1-0.4096)=295.2\), all matching. As \(n\) grows, \(0.8^n\to0\), so the amounts approach \(500\) mg: the dose never builds up without limit, because the body removes more each day as the level rises. (Proof that the formula is correct for all \(n\): Example 10.1.33.)

items.title: Group 6: Partial sums
items.text:
Example 10.1.30: A telescoping series with step \(2\)

Find \(S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\dfrac1{(2k-1)(2k+1)}\) and the sum of the series.

Solution. Partial fractions: \(\dfrac1{(2k-1)(2k+1)}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1{2k-1}-\dfrac1{2k+1}\right)\), since the bracket equals \(\dfrac{(2k+1)-(2k-1)}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}=\dfrac2{(2k-1)(2k+1)}\). The sum telescopes:

\[S_n=\frac12\left[\left(1-\frac13\right)+\left(\frac13-\frac15\right)+\cdots+\left(\frac1{2n-1}-\frac1{2n+1}\right)\right]=\frac12\left(1-\frac1{2n+1}\right)=\frac n{2n+1}.\]

Check with \(n=3\): \(\frac11\!\cdot\!\frac13+\frac13\!\cdot\!\frac15+\frac15\!\cdot\!\frac17=\frac13+\frac1{15}+\frac1{35}=\frac37\), and \(\frac3{2\cdot3+1}=\frac37\). Since \(\frac n{2n+1}\to\frac12\), the series converges to \(\frac12\).

Example 10.1.31: A geometric series

Find \(S_n\) for \(\sum_{k=1}^n5\left(\frac23\right)^{k-1}\), check \(S_4\), and decide what the series adds up to.

Solution. With \(a=5\) and \(r=\frac23\) the finite geometric sum gives

\[S_n=5\cdot\frac{1-(2/3)^n}{1-2/3}=15\left(1-\left(\frac23\right)^n\right).\]

Directly, \(S_4=5\left(1+\frac23+\frac49+\frac8{27}\right)=5\cdot\frac{65}{27}=\frac{325}{27}\), and the formula gives \(15\left(1-\frac{16}{81}\right)=15\cdot\frac{65}{81}=\frac{325}{27}\).  \(\checkmark\) Because \((2/3)^n\to0\), \(S_n\to15\), so the series converges and its sum is \(15\).

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 10.1.32: Induction: the sum of the first \(n\) odd numbers

Prove that \(1+3+5+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^2\) for every integer \(n\ge1\).

Proof. Base case \(n=1\): the left side is \(1\) and the right side is \(1^2=1\).

Inductive step. Assume the formula holds for some \(n\ge1\), that is \(1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^2\). The next term is \(2(n+1)-1=2n+1\). Adding it to both sides,

\[1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)+(2n+1)=n^2+2n+1=(n+1)^2 ,\]

which is the formula for \(n+1\). By induction the formula holds for all \(n\ge1\). ◻ ∎

In terms of partial sums, this says the series \(1+3+5+\cdots\) has \(S_n=n^2\), and then Theorem 10.1.14 recovers \(a_n=n^2-(n-1)^2=2n-1\).

Example 10.1.33: Induction on a recurrence

Prove that if \(D_1=100\) and \(D_{n+1}=0.8D_n+100\), then \(D_n=500(1-0.8^n)\) for all \(n\ge1\).

Proof. Base case \(n=1\): \(500(1-0.8)=500(0.2)=100=D_1\).

Inductive step. Assume \(D_n=500(1-0.8^n)\). Then

\[\begin{aligned} D_{n+1}&=0.8D_n+100=0.8\cdot500(1-0.8^n)+100\\ &=400-500(0.8^{n+1})+100=500-500(0.8^{n+1})=500\left(1-0.8^{n+1}\right), \end{aligned}\]

using \(0.8\cdot0.8^n=0.8^{n+1}\) and \(0.8\cdot500=400\). This is the formula for \(n+1\), so by induction it holds for all \(n\ge1\). ◻ ∎

This is the formula guessed in Example 10.1.29; the proof shows that it was not an accident of the first four terms. A general formula of this type is proved in Section 10.2.

items.title: 10.2 Sequences
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

In Definition 10.1.10 we estimated limits from tables and warned that tables prove nothing (Pause and think 10.1.2). Two questions now need honest answers. First, what does “the terms get and stay as close as we like to \(L\)” mean in a sentence that can be checked? Second, once we have that, how do we compute limits without a table: by combining limits we already know, by trapping a sequence between two others, by recognising which of two competing quantities grows faster, and, for a sequence defined by a recurrence, by deciding whether it settles down at all before we go looking for where?

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • state the \(\varepsilon\)–\(N\) definition of a limit and use it to show that a simple sequence converges or diverges;

  • compute limits of sequences with the limit laws, with limits of functions as \(x\to\infty\), with the Squeeze Theorem and by applying a continuous function to a limit;

  • find the limit of \(r^n\) for every \(r\) and compare the growth of \(\ln^q n\), \(n^p\), \(b^n\), \(n!\) and \(n^n\);

  • decide whether a sequence is bounded and whether it is monotonic, and use the Monotone Convergence Theorem to prove convergence;

  • find the limit of a recursively defined sequence by the fixed-point rule after showing that it converges, and solve \(a_{n+1}=ra_n+d\) in closed form;

  • prove the main theorems of this section.

items.title: The definition of a limit
items.text:
Definition 10.2.1: Limit of a sequence

The sequence \(\{a_n\}\) converges to \(L\), written \(\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=L\), if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an integer \(N\) such that

\[|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\quad\text{for every } n>N.\]

A sequence that does not converge diverges. We write \(\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=\infty\) if for every real number \(K\) there is an integer \(N\) with \(a_n>K\) for all \(n>N\) (and \(-\infty\) similarly); such a sequence diverges, and we say it diverges to infinity.

Read it as a game. Someone names a tolerance \(\varepsilon\), however small. You must answer with a cutoff \(N\) such that every term after the \(N\)th is within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\). If you can always win, the sequence converges to \(L\). A smaller \(\varepsilon\) usually forces a larger \(N\). This is the precise form of Definition 10.1.10, and it is the definition used in Appendix B (Definition A.2), where all the limit facts of this section are proved from it.

Example 10.2.2: Winning the game

Prove that \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^2+1}{2n^2-1}=\frac12\) and find an \(N\) that works for \(\varepsilon=0.01\).

Plan. Simplify \(|a_n-L|\) to something we can make small by choosing \(n\) large.

Solution. For \(n\ge1\),

\[\left|\frac{n^2+1}{2n^2-1}-\frac12\right|=\left|\frac{2(n^2+1)-(2n^2-1)}{2(2n^2-1)}\right|=\frac{3}{2(2n^2-1)} .\]

This is less than \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(2n^2-1>\frac3{2\varepsilon}\). Given any \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N\) an integer with \(N^2>\frac{3}{4\varepsilon}+\frac12\); then every \(n>N\) has \(2n^2-1>\frac3{2\varepsilon}\) and so \(|a_n-\frac12|<\varepsilon\). That proves the limit.

For \(\varepsilon=0.01\) we need \(2n^2-1>150\), so \(n^2>75.5\) and \(n\ge9\): \(N=8\) works. Check: at \(n=9\) the distance is \(\frac3{2\cdot161}\approx0.0093<0.01\), while at \(n=8\) it is \(\frac3{2\cdot127}\approx0.0118>0.01\), so \(N=7\) would not do.

Note that if \(N\) works for a given \(\varepsilon\), so does every larger integer, since the inequality \(|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\) is required for all \(n>N\). The definition therefore asks only that some cutoff exists, not the smallest one.

items.title: Computing limits
items.text:
Theorem 10.2.3: Limit laws

Let \(a_n o A\) and \(b_n o B\), and let \(c\) be a constant. Then \(a_n\pm b_n o A\pm B\), \(ca_n o cA\), \(a_nb_n o AB\), and \(a_n/b_n o A/B\) if \(B e0\).

Proof. Here is the proof of the sum; the other three use the same idea and are done in full in Theorem B.4. Let \(\varepsilon>0\) and choose \(N_1,N_2\) with \(|a_n-A|<\varepsilon/2\) for \(n>N_1\) and \(|b_n-B|<\varepsilon/2\) for \(n>N_2\). For \(n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}\), the triangle inequality gives \(|(a_n+b_n)-(A+B)|\le|a_n-A|+|b_n-B|<\varepsilon\). For the product the new idea is the identity \(a_nb_n-AB=a_n(b_n-B)+B(a_n-A)\), together with the fact that a convergent sequence is bounded (Theorem B.2); for the quotient one shows first that \(1/b_n o1/B\). ◻ ∎

Theorem 10.2.4: Limits of \(f(n)\)

If \(f(n)=a_n\) for every positive integer \(n\) and \(\lim_{x o\infty}f(x)=L\) (where \(L\) is a number, \(\infty\) or \(-\infty\)), then \(\lim_{n o\infty}a_n=L\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(f(x) o L\) as \(x o\infty\), there is a number \(X\) with \(|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\) for all \(x>X\). Choose an integer \(N\ge X\). For \(n>N\) we have \(n>X\), so \(|a_n-L|=|f(n)-L|<\varepsilon\). The cases \(L=\pm\infty\) are the same with “\(f(x)>K\)” or “\(f(x)<K\)” in place of “\(|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\)”. ◻ ∎

The converse is false: \(a_n=\cos(2\pi n)=1\) converges although \(\lim_{x o\infty}\cos(2\pi x)\) does not exist. So this theorem lets us use Calculus I tools (such as l’Hôpital’s Rule) on a function, but a failure for the function says nothing about the sequence.

Theorem 10.2.5: Squeeze Theorem for sequences

If \(a_n\le b_n\le c_n\) for all \(n\) beyond some index, and \(a_n o L\) and \(c_n o L\), then \(b_n o L\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon>0\) and choose \(N\) so that \(|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\) and \(|c_n-L|<\varepsilon\) (and the inequalities \(a_n\le b_n\le c_n\) hold) for \(n>N\). Then \(L-\varepsilon<a_n\le b_n\le c_n<L+\varepsilon\), so \(|b_n-L|<\varepsilon\). ◻ ∎

Theorem 10.2.6: A continuous function of a limit

If \(a_n o L\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(L\) and defined at every \(a_n\), then \(f(a_n) o f(L)\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). By continuity there is \(\delta>0\) with \(|f(y)-f(L)|<\varepsilon\) whenever \(|y-L|<\delta\). Choose \(N\) with \(|a_n-L|<\delta\) for \(n>N\). Then \(|f(a_n)-f(L)|<\varepsilon\) for \(n>N\). ◻ ∎

A consequence used constantly: \(|a_n| o0\) if and only if \(a_n o0\) (Pause and think 10.2.1 and Example 10.2.35 use related ideas), since \(|a_n-0|= ig||a_n|-0 ig|\).

Example 10.2.7: Limit laws on a rational expression

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty} rac{3n^2+n}{2n^2-5}\).

Solution. Each of \(3n^2+n\) and \(2n^2-5\) tends to infinity, so the limit laws cannot be applied directly (“\(\infty/\infty\)”). Divide numerator and denominator by the highest power, \(n^2\):

\[ rac{3n^2+n}{2n^2-5}= rac{3+1/n}{2-5/n^2}\ \longrightarrow\ rac{3+0}{2-0}= rac32,\]

using \( rac1n o0\) and \( rac5{n^2} o0\), the sum, product and quotient laws, and \(2 e0\).

Example 10.2.8: A difference of square roots

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty}\left(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n ight)\).

Solution. This is “\(\infty-\infty\)”. Multiply and divide by the conjugate \(\sqrt{n^2+n}+n\):

\[\sqrt{n^2+n}-n= rac{(n^2+n)-n^2}{\sqrt{n^2+n}+n}= rac{n}{\sqrt{n^2+n}+n}= rac{1}{\sqrt{1+1/n}+1}\ \longrightarrow\ rac1{1+1}= rac12 .\]

In the last step we used that the square root is continuous (Theorem 10.2.6) so \(\sqrt{1+1/n} o\sqrt1=1\).

Example 10.2.9: A limit of \(f(n)\)

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty}n\sin rac1n\).

Solution. Let \(f(x)=x\sin rac1x\). Substitute \(u= rac1x\); as \(x o\infty\), \(u o0^+\), and \(f(x)=\dfrac{\sin u}{u} o1\) by the basic limit from Calculus I. By Theorem 10.2.4, \(\lim_{n o\infty}n\sin rac1n=1\).

Example 10.2.10: Squeezing an oscillation

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty} rac{\cos n}{n^2}\).

Solution. The numerator oscillates, so the quotient law does not apply (it needs \(\lim\cos n\) to exist). Instead, \(-1\le\cos n\le1\) gives

\[- rac1{n^2}\le rac{\cos n}{n^2}\le rac1{n^2},\]

and both outer sequences tend to \(0\) (Theorem 10.2.4 with \(f(x)=1/x^2\)). By the Squeeze Theorem the limit is \(0\).

Knowledge Check 10.2.1: Computing limits

Find each limit or say that it diverges: (a) \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty} rac{4n^3-n}{2n^3+7}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty}\left(\sqrt{n+3}-\sqrt n ight)\); (c) \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty} rac{n^2-1}{n+2}\).

Pause and think 10.2.1: When limit laws need hypotheses

(a) Give sequences \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) that both diverge while \(a_n+b_n\) and \(a_nb_n\) both converge. (b) If \(a_n\) diverges and \(a_n+b_n\) converges, must \(b_n\) diverge? Prove your answer using a limit law. (c) Why does the quotient law in Theorem 10.2.3 require \(B e0\), and what can happen when \(A=B=0\)?

Answer and discussion

(a) \(a_n=(-1)^n\) and \(b_n=-(-1)^n\): both diverge, \(a_n+b_n=0\) converges, and with \(b_n=(-1)^n\) the product \(a_nb_n=1\) converges. (b) Yes. If \(b_n\) converged, then \(a_n=(a_n+b_n)-b_n\) would converge by the difference law, contradicting the assumption. (c) The quotient law needs \(B e0\) since division by \(0\) is undefined and \(b_n\) may be \(0\) or tiny; when \(A=B=0\) the quotient can do anything: \( rac1n ig/ rac1n o1\), \( rac1{n^2} ig/ rac1n o0\), \( rac1n ig/ rac1{n^2} o\infty\). (This is the “\(0/0\)” form.)

items.title: Geometric sequences and growth rates
items.text:
Theorem 10.2.11: The sequence \(r^n\)

Let \(r\) be a real number. Then

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}r^n=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if } |r|<1,\\ 1 & \text{if } r=1,\end{cases}\]

\(r^n\to\infty\) if \(r>1\), and \(\{r^n\}\) diverges if \(r\le-1\).

Proof. We use Bernoulli’s inequality: \((1+h)^n\ge1+nh\) for every \(h>0\) and every integer \(n\ge1\). This is proved by induction (Example 10.2.34).

Case \(r>1\). Write \(r=1+h\) with \(h>0\). Then \(r^n\ge1+nh\), and \(1+nh\to\infty\), so \(r^n\to\infty\) (given \(K\), choose \(N\ge K/h\); for \(n>N\), \(r^n\ge1+nh>K\)).

Case \(0<|r|<1\). Then \(1/|r|>1\); write \(1/|r|=1+h\) with \(h>0\). Then \(|r|^n=\dfrac1{(1+h)^n}\le\dfrac1{1+nh}\), so

\[0\le|r^n|\le\frac1{1+nh}\to0,\]

and the Squeeze Theorem gives \(|r^n|\to0\), hence \(r^n\to0\). For \(r=0\) the sequence is \(0,0,\dots\) and the claim is trivial.

Case \(r=1\). The sequence is constant, equal to \(1\).

Case \(r=-1\). The terms alternate between \(-1\) and \(1\); consecutive terms differ by \(2\), so no limit exists (the argument of Appendix Example B.9).

Case \(r<-1\). Then \(|r|>1\), so \(|r^n|=|r|^n\to\infty\) by the first case; a sequence with \(|a_n|\to\infty\) is unbounded, but a convergent sequence is bounded (Theorem B.2), so \(\{r^n\}\) diverges. ◻ ∎

Example 10.2.12: Using \(r^n\)

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3^n+2^n}{3^{n+1}}\).

Solution. Divide each term by \(3^n\) and write \(3^{n+1}=3\cdot3^n\):

\[\frac{3^n+2^n}{3^{n+1}}=\frac{1+(2/3)^n}{3}\ \longrightarrow\ \frac{1+0}{3}=\frac13,\]

because \(|2/3|<1\), so \((2/3)^n\to0\) by Theorem 10.2.11.

Which grows faster, \(n^{10}\) or \(1.01^n\)? Or \(2^n\) or \(n!\)? The next theorem ranks the standard growth rates; each statement says that the second quantity eventually dwarfs the first.

Theorem 10.2.13: Growth rates

Let \(p>0\), \(q>0\) and \(b>1\). Then

(a) \(\dfrac{(\ln n)^q}{n^p}\to0\),

(b) \(\dfrac{n^p}{b^n}\to0\),

(c) \(\dfrac{b^n}{n!}\to0\),

(d) \(\dfrac{n!}{n^n}\to0\).

Consequently, for large \(n\),

\[(\ln n)^q\ll n^p\ll b^n\ll n!\ll n^n,\]

where \(u_n\ll v_n\) means \(u_n/v_n\to0\).

Proof. (d) \(\dfrac{n!}{n^n}=\dfrac1n\cdot\dfrac2n\cdots\dfrac nn\le\dfrac1n\cdot1\cdots1=\dfrac1n\), since each of the other factors is at most \(1\). So \(0<\frac{n!}{n^n}\le\frac1n\to0\), and the Squeeze Theorem gives the limit \(0\).

(c) Choose an integer \(M\ge2b\). For \(n>M\),

\[\frac{b^n}{n!}=\frac{b^M}{M!}\cdot\frac{b}{M+1}\cdot\frac{b}{M+2}\cdots\frac bn\le\frac{b^M}{M!}\left(\frac12\right)^{n-M},\]

because each of the \(n-M\) factors \(\frac bj\) (\(j>M\)) is at most \(\frac b{2b}=\frac12\). The right side is a constant times \((1/2)^n\), which tends to \(0\) by Theorem 10.2.11; squeezing gives \(b^n/n!\to0\).

(b) Write \(b=1+h\) with \(h>0\) and choose an integer \(m>p\). For \(n\ge2m\) the binomial theorem gives, keeping only one term,

\[b^n\ge\binom nm h^m=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-m+1)}{m!}h^m\ge\frac{(n/2)^m}{m!}h^m ,\]

since each of the \(m\) factors \(n-j\) (\(0\le j\le m-1\)) is at least \(n-m+1>n/2\) when \(n\ge2m\). Hence

\[0<\frac{n^p}{b^n}\le\frac{2^m\,m!}{h^m}\cdot n^{p-m}\to0,\]

because \(p-m<0\) means \(n^{p-m}=1/n^{m-p}\to0\) (Theorem 10.2.4). The Squeeze Theorem gives (b).

(a) First take \(q=1\). The function \(f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x^p}\) has the form \(\infty/\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\), and by l’Hôpital’s Rule

\[\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln x}{x^p}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1/x}{p\,x^{p-1}}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac1{p\,x^{p}}=0,\]

so \(\frac{\ln n}{n^p}\to0\) for every \(p>0\) by Theorem 10.2.4. For general \(q>0\) apply this with \(p/q\) in place of \(p\): \(\frac{(\ln n)^q}{n^p}=\left(\frac{\ln n}{n^{p/q}}\right)^q\to0^q=0\), using Theorem 10.2.6 with the continuous function \(y\mapsto y^q\) at \(0\) (continuous from the right at \(0\), which is all that is needed since the terms are positive).

The chain follows by combining (a)–(d): for instance \(n^p/n!=\frac{n^p}{b^n}\cdot\frac{b^n}{n!}\) with \(b=2\) is a product of two sequences tending to \(0\). ◻ ∎

Example 10.2.14: Ranking growth rates in a quotient

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n!+4^n}{n!+n^4}\).

Solution. The dominant term in both numerator and denominator is \(n!\). Divide by \(n!\):

\[\frac{n!+4^n}{n!+n^4}=\frac{1+4^n/n!}{1+n^4/n!}\ \longrightarrow\ \frac{1+0}{1+0}=1,\]

because \(4^n/n!\to0\) by Theorem 10.2.13(c), and \(n^4/n!\to0\) because \(n^4/2^n\to0\) by (b) and \(2^n/n!\to0\) by (c). Numerically, \(4^{10}/10!\approx0.29\) and \(4^{20}/20!\approx4.5\times10^{-7}\), already small.

Knowledge Check 10.2.2: Squeeze and growth

Find each limit: (a) \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{(-1)^n\,n}{n^2+1}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2^n+5^n}{5^n+1}\); (c) \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^{20}}{1.5^n}\) and say what a table of the first \(50\) terms would show.

items.title: Monotone sequences and boundedness
items.text:
Definition 10.2.15: Monotone and bounded sequences

A sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is nondecreasing if \(a_{n+1}\ge a_n\) for all \(n\), increasing if \(a_{n+1}>a_n\), and nonincreasing or decreasing if the inequalities are reversed; it is monotonic if it is of one of these kinds. It is bounded above if there is \(M\) with \(a_n\le M\) for all \(n\), bounded below if \(a_n\ge m\) for all \(n\), and bounded if both hold.

To show a sequence is monotonic, compare \(a_{n+1}\) with \(a_n\) directly (by subtraction, by a ratio of positive terms, or, for \(a_n=f(n)\), from the sign of \(f'\)), or use induction on a recurrence. Bounds are usually proved by induction or by an inequality.

Theorem 10.2.16: Monotone Convergence Theorem

A nondecreasing sequence that is bounded above converges, to its least upper bound. A nonincreasing sequence that is bounded below converges, to its greatest lower bound. In particular a bounded monotonic sequence converges.

Proof. Let \(\{a_n\}\) be nondecreasing and bounded above. By the completeness of the real numbers (the least upper bound property; see the beginning of Appendix A) the set \(\{a_1,a_2,\dots\}\) has a least upper bound \(L\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(L-\varepsilon\) is not an upper bound, some \(a_N>L-\varepsilon\). For \(n>N\) we have \(a_n\ge a_N>L-\varepsilon\) because the sequence is nondecreasing, and \(a_n\le L\) because \(L\) is an upper bound. So \(|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\). The nonincreasing case follows by applying this to \(-a_n\). The complete argument is Theorem A.5. ◻ ∎

The theorem does not tell us the limit; it tells us there is one. For a recurrence, there is a good way to find it once existence is known.

Theorem 10.2.17: Fixed-point rule

Suppose \(a_{n+1}=f(a_n)\) for all \(n\), the function \(f\) is continuous, and \(a_n\to L\). Then \(f(L)=L\).

Proof. The sequence \(a_2,a_3,\dots\) also converges to \(L\) (it is the same sequence with the first term removed; Theorem B.3). On the other hand \(a_{n+1}=f(a_n)\to f(L)\) by Theorem 10.2.6. A sequence has only one limit (Theorem B.1), so \(f(L)=L\). ◻ ∎

The rule assumes the limit exists

The fixed-point rule says if the sequence converges then the limit solves \(f(L)=L\). It never says that the sequence converges. The sequence \(a_1=1\), \(a_{n+1}=2a_n+1\) gives \(L=2L+1\), so \(L=-1\), yet the terms \(1,3,7,15,\dots\) grow without bound: there is no limit at all (Pause and think 10.2.3). Prove convergence (monotone and bounded) first, then solve for \(L\).

Example 10.2.18: Monotone and bounded: repeated square roots

In Example 10.1.23 we guessed that \(a_1=1\), \(a_{n+1}=\sqrt{6+a_n}\) tends to \(3\). Prove it.

Bounded above by \(3\). \(a_1=1<3\). If \(a_n<3\) then \(a_{n+1}=\sqrt{6+a_n}<\sqrt{9}=3\). So \(a_n<3\) for all \(n\) (induction).

Increasing. Compare squares: \(a_{n+1}^2-a_n^2=6+a_n-a_n^2=(3-a_n)(2+a_n)>0\), because \(a_n<3\) and \(a_n>0\). Hence \(a_{n+1}>a_n\) for every \(n\) (all terms are positive).

Limit. By the Monotone Convergence Theorem the sequence converges, say to \(L\), and \(L\le3\). By the fixed-point rule with \(f(x)=\sqrt{6+x}\), \(L=\sqrt{6+L}\), so \(L^2-L-6=(L-3)(L+2)=0\); since \(L>0\), \(L=3\).

Pause and think 10.2.2: Which hypothesis does the work?

The Monotone Convergence Theorem has two hypotheses: “monotonic” and “bounded”. Give an example of (a) a monotonic sequence that is not bounded and diverges, and (b) a bounded sequence that is not monotonic and diverges. Then say, in words, why each hypothesis cannot be dropped.

Answer and discussion

(a) \(a_n=n\): increasing, unbounded, diverges to infinity. (b) \(a_n=(-1)^n\): bounded, not monotonic, diverges. The monotonic hypothesis prevents oscillation between two values; the bounded hypothesis prevents escape to infinity. The theorem needs both: monotone says the terms can only move one way, and bounded says they cannot move forever.

items.title: Recurrences \(a_{n+1}=ra_n+d\)
items.text:
Theorem 10.2.19: Linear recurrences of first order

Let \(a_{n+1}=ra_n+d\) for all \(n\ge1\), with \(r\ne1\), and let \(L=\dfrac d{1-r}\). Then

\[a_n=L+(a_1-L)\,r^{\,n-1}\quad\text{for every } n\ge1 .\]

Consequently the sequence converges if \(|r|<1\) (to \(L\)) or if \(a_1=L\) (it is constant), and otherwise it diverges.

Proof. Note that \(L\) satisfies \(L=rL+d\), because \(L(1-r)=d\). By induction: for \(n=1\) the formula says \(a_1=L+(a_1-L)=a_1\). If \(a_n=L+(a_1-L)r^{n-1}\), then

\[a_{n+1}=ra_n+d=rL+(a_1-L)r^{n}+d=\big(rL+d\big)+(a_1-L)r^n=L+(a_1-L)r^{n},\]

which is the formula for \(n+1\). For the consequence, if \(|r|<1\) then \(r^{n-1}\to0\) by Theorem 10.2.11, so \(a_n\to L\). If \(a_1=L\) the formula gives \(a_n=L\) for all \(n\). If \(|r|\ge1\) and \(a_1\ne L\), the sequence \((a_1-L)r^{n-1}\) diverges by Theorem 10.2.11 (for \(r=-1\) it alternates; for \(|r|>1\) it is unbounded; \(r=1\) is excluded), so \(a_n=L+(a_1-L)r^{n-1}\) diverges (if \(a_n\) converged then so would \(a_n-L\)). ◻ ∎

Example 10.2.20: Solving a linear recurrence

In Example 10.1.29 the amount of a drug just after the \(n\)th dose satisfied \(D_1=100\), \(D_{n+1}=0.8D_n+100\). Find \(\lim D_n\).

Solution. Here \(r=0.8\), \(d=100\), so \(L=\dfrac{100}{1-0.8}=500\) and by Theorem 10.2.19

\[D_n=500+(100-500)(0.8)^{n-1}=500-400(0.8)^{n-1}.\]

This agrees with the closed form \(500(1-0.8^n)\) found earlier (since \(400\cdot0.8^{n-1}=500\cdot0.8^n\)). Because \(|0.8|<1\), \(D_n\to500\).

Knowledge Check 10.2.3: A first-order recurrence

Let \(a_1=1\) and \(a_{n+1}=\dfrac{a_n+3}{2}\). (a) Find \(L=\dfrac d{1-r}\) and the closed form of \(a_n\). (b) Find \(\lim a_n\). (c) For the recurrence \(b_1=2\), \(b_{n+1}=-2b_n+3\), find \(L\), the closed form, and say whether \(b_n\) converges.

Pause and think 10.2.3: Why does the fixed-point rule give a false answer here?

Apply the fixed-point rule to \(a_1=1\), \(a_{n+1}=2a_n+1\) and find \(L\). All the terms are positive. What does that say? Use Theorem 10.2.19 to decide what really happens, and say which hypothesis of the rule was false.

Answer and discussion

The rule gives \(L=2L+1\), so \(L=-1\). But all terms are positive, and a limit of positive numbers cannot be negative (see the remark on limits and inequalities), so something is wrong. Here \(r=2\), \(d=1\), \(L=\frac1{1-2}=-1\), and \(a_n=-1+(1-(-1))2^{n-1}=-1+2^n\), which tends to infinity. The hypothesis that failed is that \(a_n\) converges. The equation \(L=f(L)\) only locates the possible limits.

Example 10.2.21: Newton’s method for \(\sqrt5\)

Let \(a_1=3\) and \(a_{n+1}=\dfrac12\left(a_n+\dfrac5{a_n}\right)\). Show that \(\{a_n\}\) converges and find its limit.

Bounded below by \(\sqrt5\). For \(a_n>0\), \(a_{n+1}-\sqrt5=\dfrac{(a_n-\sqrt5)^2}{2a_n}\ge0\). [To check: \(\frac12\left(a+\frac5a\right)-\sqrt5=\frac{a^2-2\sqrt5a+5}{2a}\).] So \(a_n\ge\sqrt5\) for all \(n\ge2\), and \(a_1=3>\sqrt5\) too.

Nonincreasing. Since \(a_n^2\ge5\), we have \(\dfrac5{a_n}\le a_n\), so \(a_{n+1}-a_n=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac5{a_n}-a_n\right)\le0\).

Limit. By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, \(a_n\to L\ge\sqrt5\). The fixed-point rule with \(f(x)=\frac12(x+5/x)\) (continuous for \(x>0\)) gives \(L=\frac12(L+\frac5L)\), so \(L^2=5\) and \(L=\sqrt5\approx2.2360680\). The first terms \(3,\ \frac73\approx2.3333,\ \frac{47}{21}\approx2.2381\) converge very quickly.

Limits and inequalities

If \(a_n\to L\) and \(a_n\ge m\) for all \(n\), then \(L\ge m\). (Suppose instead \(L<m\) and take \(\varepsilon=m-L>0\); for large \(n\), \(a_n<L+\varepsilon=m\), a contradiction.) But strict inequalities are not preserved: \(a_n=\frac1n>0\) for all \(n\), yet \(\lim a_n=0\), which is not greater than \(0\).

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  1. Limit laws and algebra (Examples 10.2.22–10.2.23).

  2. Limits of \(f(n)\) and the Squeeze Theorem (Examples 10.2.24–10.2.25).

  3. Geometric sequences and growth rates (Examples 10.2.26–10.2.27).

  4. Recurrences \(a_{n+1}=ra_n+d\) (Examples 10.2.28–10.2.29).

  5. Monotone and bounded (Examples 10.2.30–10.2.31).

  6. The \(\varepsilon\)–\(N\) definition (Examples 10.2.32–10.2.33).

  7. Proofs (Examples 10.2.34–10.2.35).

items.title: Group 1: Limit laws and algebra
items.text:
Example 10.2.22: A rational expression with a lower-order tail

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{5n^2-3}{n^2+4n}\).

Solution. Divide the numerator and the denominator by \(n^2\), the highest power in the denominator: \(\dfrac{5-3/n^2}{1+4/n}\). Since \(\frac3{n^2}\to0\) and \(\frac4n\to0\), the limit laws give \(\dfrac{5-0}{1+0}=5\). Check: \(a_{1000}=\dfrac{5\cdot10^6-3}{10^6+4000}\approx4.9801\), below \(5\), as expected since the \(4n\) in the denominator pulls the value down.

Example 10.2.23: A hidden conjugate

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\sqrt{n^2+3n}-n\right)\).

Solution. Each term tends to infinity, so we use the conjugate: \(\sqrt{n^2+3n}-n=\dfrac{3n}{\sqrt{n^2+3n}+n}=\dfrac3{\sqrt{1+3/n}+1}\to\dfrac3{1+1}=\dfrac32\). Check: at \(n=10^4\), \(\sqrt{10^8+3\cdot10^4}-10^4\approx1.4999\).

items.title: Group 2: Limits of \(f(n)\) and the Squeeze Theorem
items.text:
Example 10.2.24: A derivative in disguise

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}n\left(e^{1/n}-1\right)\).

Solution. Let \(f(x)=x\left(e^{1/x}-1\right)=\dfrac{e^{u}-1}{u}\) with \(u=\frac1x\to0^+\). This is the difference quotient of \(e^u\) at \(u=0\), whose limit is the derivative \(\frac{d}{du}e^u\big|_{u=0}=1\). By Theorem 10.2.4, the sequence tends to \(1\). Check: at \(n=1000\), \(1000\left(e^{0.001}-1\right)\approx1.0005\).

Example 10.2.25: Squeezing with a bounded oscillation

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n+\sin n}{n+2}\).

Solution. Because \(-1\le\sin n\le1\), \(\dfrac{n-1}{n+2}\le\dfrac{n+\sin n}{n+2}\le\dfrac{n+1}{n+2}\). Both bounds tend to \(1\) (divide by \(n\): \(\frac{1-1/n}{1+2/n}\) and \(\frac{1+1/n}{1+2/n}\)). By the Squeeze Theorem the limit is \(1\). Notice that we could not split the fraction as \(\frac{n}{n+2}+\frac{\sin n}{n+2}\) and apply the sum law unless we knew each piece converges; here they do (\(\frac{\sin n}{n+2}\to0\) by squeezing), but the squeeze above avoids the extra step.

items.title: Group 3: Geometric sequences and growth rates
items.text:
Example 10.2.26: Dominant exponentials

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3^n-2^n}{3^n+2^n}\).

Solution. Divide by \(3^n\): \(\dfrac{1-(2/3)^n}{1+(2/3)^n}\). Since \((2/3)^n\to0\) (Theorem 10.2.11), the limit is \(\dfrac{1-0}{1+0}=1\). Check at \(n=10\): \(\frac{3^{10}-2^{10}}{3^{10}+2^{10}}=\frac{58025}{60073}\approx0.966\).

Example 10.2.27: Factorials win eventually

(a) Show that \(\dfrac{n^{10}}{1.01^n}\to0\). (b) Find where \(a_n=\dfrac{100^n}{n!}\) stops increasing, and explain why \(a_n\to0\) anyway.

Solution. (a) This is Theorem 10.2.13(b) with \(p=10\) and \(b=1.01\): any exponential beats any power, however small the base excess. (It takes a very large \(n\): \(\frac{n^{10}}{1.01^n}\) is still huge at \(n=1000\), so a table of moderate size would suggest the opposite. Compare Pause and think 10.1.2.)

(b) The ratio of consecutive terms is \(\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{100^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{100^n/n!}=\dfrac{100}{n+1}\), which is greater than \(1\) while \(n+1<100\), equal to \(1\) at \(n=99\), and less than \(1\) afterwards. So the terms increase up to \(a_{99}\), with \(a_{100}=a_{99}\), and then decrease. Indeed \(\frac{100^{100}}{100!}=\frac{100^{99}}{99!}\cdot\frac{100}{100}\). The maximum is astronomically large (\(a_{99}\approx10^{42}\)), yet by Theorem 10.2.13(c) with \(b=100\) the sequence tends to \(0\). The theorem is about the long run only.

items.title: Group 4: Recurrences \(a_{n+1}=ra_n+d\)
items.text:
Example 10.2.28: A convergent linear recurrence

Let \(a_1=10\) and \(a_{n+1}=\frac12a_n+4\). Find \(a_n\) in closed form and its limit.

Solution. Here \(r=\frac12\), \(d=4\), \(L=\dfrac4{1-1/2}=8\), so Theorem 10.2.19 gives \(a_n=8+(10-8)\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}=8+2\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}\). Check: \(a_2=8+1=9\) and directly \(\frac12(10)+4=9\); \(a_3=8+\frac12=8.5\) and directly \(\frac12(9)+4=8.5\). As \(n\to\infty\), \(\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}\to0\) and \(a_n\to8\), decreasing from above.

Example 10.2.29: When \(|r|>1\)

Let \(a_{n+1}=-2a_n+3\). For which starting values \(a_1\) does \(\{a_n\}\) converge? Find the limit.

Solution. \(r=-2\), \(d=3\), \(L=\dfrac3{1-(-2)}=1\), so \(a_n=1+(a_1-1)(-2)^{n-1}\). Since \(|r|>1\), the term \((a_1-1)(-2)^{n-1}\) diverges unless \(a_1-1=0\). So the sequence converges only if \(a_1=1\), when it is constant \(1,1,1,\dots\) with limit \(1\). For example \(a_1=2\) gives \(2,\,-1,\,5,\,-7,\,17,\dots\) with \(a_n=1+(-2)^{n-1}\): the terms alternate in sign and grow. Check: \(a_2=-4+3=-1\), formula \(1+(-2)=-1\); \(a_3=2+3=5\), formula \(1+4=5\). So the fixed point \(L=1\) is repelling: a start anywhere else is pushed away (compare the warning about the fixed-point rule).

items.title: Group 5: Monotone and bounded
items.text:
Example 10.2.30: A series-like sequence bounded by a geometric sum

Let \(a_n=1+1+\frac1{2!}+\frac1{3!}+\cdots+\frac1{n!}=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac1{k!}\). Show that \(\{a_n\}\) converges.

Solution. Increasing: \(a_{n+1}-a_n=\frac1{(n+1)!}>0\). Bounded: for \(k\ge1\), \(k!=1\cdot2\cdot3\cdots k\ge2^{k-1}\) (each factor from \(2\) on is at least \(2\)), so \(\frac1{k!}\le\frac1{2^{k-1}}\) and

\[a_n\le1+\left(1+\frac12+\frac14+\cdots+\frac1{2^{n-1}}\right)=1+\frac{1-2^{-n}}{1-\frac12}<1+2=3 ,\]

using the finite geometric sum (Theorem 10.1.15). By the Monotone Convergence Theorem the sequence converges, to a number between \(a_3=\frac{8}{3}\approx2.667\) and \(3\). (It converges to \(e\).)

Example 10.2.31: A bounded sum by comparison with a telescoping sum

Let \(s_n=1+\dfrac1{2^2}+\dfrac1{3^2}+\cdots+\dfrac1{n^2}\). Show that \(\{s_n\}\) converges.

Solution. The sequence is increasing since each added term is positive. To bound it, compare each term with a telescoping one: for \(k\ge2\), \(\dfrac1{k^2}<\dfrac1{k(k-1)}=\dfrac1{k-1}-\dfrac1k\). Therefore

\[s_n<1+\left(1-\frac12\right)+\left(\frac12-\frac13\right)+\cdots+\left(\frac1{n-1}-\frac1n\right)=2-\frac1n<2 .\]

So \(\{s_n\}\) is increasing and bounded above by \(2\), hence convergent by the Monotone Convergence Theorem. The terms are \(1,\ 1.25,\ 1.3611,\ 1.4236,\dots\), and the limit is in fact \(\frac{\pi^2}6\approx1.6449\), a fact we cannot get from this argument alone.

items.title: Group 6: The \(\varepsilon\)–\(N\) definition
items.text:
Example 10.2.32: Finding \(N\) for a rational sequence

Prove that \(\dfrac{3n}{n+1}\to3\) and find \(N\) for \(\varepsilon=0.01\).

Solution. \(\left|\dfrac{3n}{n+1}-3\right|=\left|\dfrac{3n-3n-3}{n+1}\right|=\dfrac3{n+1}\). This is less than \(\varepsilon\) when \(n+1>\frac3\varepsilon\), that is \(n>\frac3\varepsilon-1\). So for every \(\varepsilon>0\) any integer \(N\ge\frac3\varepsilon-1\) works. For \(\varepsilon=0.01\): \(\frac3\varepsilon-1=299\), so \(N=299\). Check at \(n=300\): \(\frac3{301}<0.01\).

Example 10.2.33: An alternating sequence

Prove that \(\dfrac{(-1)^n}{n}\to0\) and find \(N\) for \(\varepsilon=0.001\).

Solution. The signs do not affect the distance: \(\left|\dfrac{(-1)^n}n-0\right|=\dfrac1n\). We need \(\frac1n<\varepsilon\), that is \(n>\frac1\varepsilon\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), take any integer \(N\ge\frac1\varepsilon\); then \(n>N\) gives \(\frac1n<\varepsilon\). For \(\varepsilon=0.001\), \(N=1000\). Check: for \(n=1001\) the distance is \(\frac1{1001}<0.001\), but at \(n=1000\) it is exactly \(0.001\), which is not less than \(\varepsilon\), so the cutoff \(N=999\) would fail: the definition requires strict inequality for every \(n>N\).

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 10.2.34: Bernoulli’s inequality

Prove that \((1+h)^n\ge1+nh\) for every real \(h>0\) and every integer \(n\ge1\).

Proof. Base case \(n=1\): \((1+h)^1=1+h\ge1+1\cdot h\).

Inductive step. Assume \((1+h)^n\ge1+nh\). Multiply both sides by \(1+h>0\) (this keeps the inequality):

\[(1+h)^{n+1}\ge(1+nh)(1+h)=1+(n+1)h+nh^2\ge1+(n+1)h,\]

because \(nh^2\ge0\). This is the statement for \(n+1\), so by induction it holds for all \(n\ge1\). ◻ ∎

The inequality is the key to Theorem 10.2.11: it says that \((1+h)^n\) grows at least linearly in \(n\).

Example 10.2.35: Absolute values and limits

Prove that if \(a_n\to L\), then \(|a_n|\to|L|\). Is the converse true?

Proof. By the reverse triangle inequality \(\big||a_n|-|L|\big|\le|a_n-L|\). (To see it, write \(|a_n|=|(a_n-L)+L|\le|a_n-L|+|L|\), so \(|a_n|-|L|\le|a_n-L|\); exchange the roles of \(a_n\) and \(L\) to get \(|L|-|a_n|\le|a_n-L|\).) Let \(\varepsilon>0\) and choose \(N\) with \(|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\) for \(n>N\). Then \(\big||a_n|-|L|\big|<\varepsilon\) for \(n>N\), which is the claim. (Alternatively, apply Theorem 10.2.6 with \(f(x)=|x|\), which is continuous.) ◻ ∎

The converse is false: \(a_n=(-1)^n\) has \(|a_n|=1\to1\), but \(\{a_n\}\) diverges. The converse does hold when the limit is zero: \(|a_n|\to0\Rightarrow a_n\to0\), as in the remark after Theorem 10.2.6.

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 10.2.1. (a) Divide by \(n^3\): \(\frac{4-1/n^2}{2+7/n^3}\to\frac42=2\). (b) Conjugate: \(\sqrt{n+3}-\sqrt n=\frac{3}{\sqrt{n+3}+\sqrt n}\to0\) since the denominator tends to infinity. (c) \(\frac{n^2-1}{n+2}=\frac{n-1/n}{1+2/n}\to\infty\) (the numerator tends to infinity and the denominator to \(1\)); the sequence diverges to infinity. Equivalently \(\frac{n^2-1}{n+2}=n-2+\frac3{n+2}\) by division.

Knowledge Check 10.2.2. (a) \(\left|\frac{(-1)^nn}{n^2+1}\right|\le\frac n{n^2+1}\to0\), so by squeezing the limit is \(0\). (b) Divide by \(5^n\): \(\frac{(2/5)^n+1}{1+5^{-n}}\to\frac{0+1}{1+0}=1\). (c) \(n^{20}/1.5^n\to0\) by Theorem 10.2.13(b), but the first \(50\) terms are large: for example \(50^{20}/1.5^{50}\approx1.5\times10^{25}\), so a table of \(50\) terms would show huge, growing values and mislead; the decrease begins only much later.

Knowledge Check 10.2.3. (a) \(r=\frac12\), \(d=\frac32\), \(L=\frac{3/2}{1/2}=3\), \(a_n=3+(1-3)\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}=3-2\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}\). Check \(a_2=\frac{1+3}2=2\) and the formula \(3-1=2\). (b) \(|r|<1\), so \(a_n\to3\). (c) \(r=-2\), \(d=3\), \(L=1\), \(b_n=1+(2-1)(-2)^{n-1}=1+(-2)^{n-1}\); since \(|r|>1\) and \(b_1\ne L\), \(b_n\) diverges.

items.title: Appendix: Sequences and Infinite Series
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

Chapter 10 leans on a few facts that its sections state and use but that need more care than a lecture allows: a bounded nondecreasing sequence converges, limits obey the usual laws, and a sequence squeezed between two sequences with the same limit has that limit. This appendix proves them. Section A starts from one assumption about the real numbers (completeness) and proves the Monotone Convergence Theorem from it. Section B uses the \(\varepsilon\)–\(N\) definition of a limit to prove the limit facts for sequences. Nothing here is needed to use the facts, only to see why they are true.

items.title: Appendix A. Completeness and the Monotone Convergence Theorem
items.text:
Definition A.1: Upper bound, supremum

Let \(S\) be a nonempty set of real numbers. A number \(M\) is an upper bound of \(S\) if \(s\le M\) for every \(s\) in \(S\); the set \(S\) is bounded above if it has an upper bound. A number \(M^*\) is the least upper bound (or supremum) of \(S\), written \(M^*=\sup S\), if

(i) \(M^*\) is an upper bound of \(S\), and

(ii) \(M^*\le M\) for every upper bound \(M\) of \(S\).

Lower bounds, bounded below and the greatest lower bound \(\inf S\) are defined in the same way with the inequalities reversed.

The supremum need not belong to the set. The set \(\{x : 0<x<1\}\) has supremum \(1\), which is not in the set, while the set \(\{x : 0<x\le 1\}\) has supremum \(1\), which is.

The Completeness Axiom

Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound.

This is an assumption about the real numbers, not a theorem: it cannot be derived from the rules of arithmetic and order, so we take it as the starting point. It is exactly what the rational numbers lack. The set of rational numbers \(q\) with \(q^2<2\) is bounded above by \(2\), but among the rational numbers it has no least upper bound. Every proof in this appendix, and the Monotone Convergence Theorem on which Chapter 10 relies, rests on it.

Definition A.2: Limit of a sequence

A sequence \(\{a_n\}\) converges to the number \(L\), written \(\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=L\), if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an integer \(N\) such that

\[\abs{a_n-L}<\varepsilon \quad\text{for every } n>N.\]

A sequence that does not converge diverges. We write \(a_n\to\infty\) if for every real number \(K\) there is an integer \(N\) such that \(a_n>K\) for every \(n>N\) (and \(a_n\to-\infty\) if \(a_n<K\) for every \(n>N\) in the same way); such a sequence diverges.

Theorem A.3: Approximation property of the supremum

Let \(S\) be nonempty and bounded above, and let \(M=\sup S\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an element \(s\) of \(S\) with \(M-\varepsilon<s\le M\).

Proof. Because \(M-\varepsilon<M\) and \(M\) is the least upper bound, the number \(M-\varepsilon\) is not an upper bound of \(S\). So some element \(s\) of \(S\) satisfies \(s>M-\varepsilon\). Also \(s\le M\), because \(M\) is an upper bound of \(S\). ◻ ∎

Theorem A.4: Archimedean property

For every real number \(x\) there is a positive integer \(n\) with \(n>x\). Consequently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a positive integer \(N\) with \(\dfrac1N<\varepsilon\).

Proof. Suppose, to the contrary, that some real number \(x\) satisfies \(n\le x\) for every positive integer \(n\). Then the set \(\N=\{1,2,3,\dots\}\) is nonempty and bounded above (by \(x\)), so by the Completeness Axiom it has a supremum \(M\). By Theorem A.3 with \(\varepsilon=1\) there is a positive integer \(n\) with \(n>M-1\). Then \(n+1\) is a positive integer and \(n+1>M\), which contradicts the fact that \(M\) is an upper bound of \(\N\). This proves the first statement.

For the second, apply the first statement to \(x=1/\varepsilon\): there is a positive integer \(N>1/\varepsilon\), and then \(1/N<\varepsilon\). ◻ ∎

Theorem A.5: Monotone Convergence Theorem

(a) If \(\{a_n\}\) is nondecreasing and bounded above, then \(\{a_n\}\) converges, and its limit is \(\sup\{a_n\}\).

(b) If \(\{a_n\}\) is nonincreasing and bounded below, then \(\{a_n\}\) converges, and its limit is \(\inf\{a_n\}\).

In particular, a bounded monotonic sequence converges.

Proof. (a) The set \(S=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots\}\) is nonempty and bounded above, so \(L=\sup S\) exists by the Completeness Axiom. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). By Theorem A.3 there is an index \(N\) with \(L-\varepsilon<a_N\le L\). For every \(n>N\) we have \(a_n\ge a_N\) because the sequence is nondecreasing, and \(a_n\le L\) because \(L\) is an upper bound. Hence

\[L-\varepsilon<a_N\le a_n\le L, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \abs{a_n-L}<\varepsilon .\]

Since \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, \(a_n\to L\).

(b) The sequence \(b_n=-a_n\) is nondecreasing, and it is bounded above by \(-m\) if \(m\) is a lower bound of \(\{a_n\}\). By part (a), \(b_n\to L'\) with \(L'=\sup\{b_n\}\). Because \(\abs{a_n-(-L')}=\abs{b_n-L'}\), we get \(a_n\to-L'\). Finally \(-L'=\inf\{a_n\}\): every \(b_n\le L'\) gives \(a_n\ge-L'\), so \(-L'\) is a lower bound; and if \(m'\) is any lower bound of \(\{a_n\}\), then \(-m'\) is an upper bound of \(\{b_n\}\), so \(L'\le -m'\), that is \(m'\le -L'\). ◻ ∎

Theorem A.6: The limit of a monotone sequence respects bounds

If \(\{a_n\}\) is nondecreasing and \(a_n\le M\) for every \(n\), then \(\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\le M\) (and \(\lim a_n\ge a_1\)). If \(\{a_n\}\) is nonincreasing and \(a_n\ge m\) for every \(n\), then \(\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\ge m\).

Proof. In the nondecreasing case the limit is \(L=\sup\{a_n\}\) by Theorem A.5. Since \(M\) is an upper bound of \(\{a_n\}\) and \(L\) is the least upper bound, \(L\le M\); and \(L\ge a_1\) because \(L\) is an upper bound. The nonincreasing case is the same argument applied to \(-a_n\). ◻ ∎

Example A.7: A supremum that is not a maximum

Let \(S=\{1-\tfrac1n : n=1,2,3,\dots\}=\{0,\tfrac12,\tfrac23,\tfrac34,\dots\}\). Show that \(\sup S=1\) and that \(S\) has no largest element.

Solution. Step 1: \(1\) is an upper bound. Every element is \(1-\frac1n\) with \(\frac1n>0\), so every element is less than \(1\).

Step 2: nothing smaller is an upper bound. Let \(M<1\). We must find an element of \(S\) bigger than \(M\). The number \(1-M\) is positive, so by the Archimedean property (Theorem A.4) there is an integer \(N\) with \(\frac1N<1-M\). Rearranging, \(1-\frac1N>M\), so \(M\) is not an upper bound. Hence every upper bound is at least \(1\), and \(\sup S=1\).

Step 3: no maximum. A maximum would be an element equal to \(\sup S=1\), but every element is strictly less than \(1\).

As a check on the answer, the elements get closer and closer to \(1\): \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\tfrac1n\right)=1\), so \(\sup S=1\).

Example A.8: Monotone Convergence in action: repeated square roots

Let \(a_1=\sqrt2\) and \(a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+a_n}\). Show that \(\{a_n\}\) converges and find its limit.

Plan. The theorem needs two facts: the sequence is monotonic and it is bounded. Terms: \(a_1\approx1.414\), \(a_2\approx1.848\), \(a_3\approx1.962\). They increase; they seem to stay below \(2\).

Bounded above by \(2\) (induction). \(a_1=\sqrt2<2\). If \(a_n<2\), then \(a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+a_n}<\sqrt{2+2}=2\), because the square root is increasing. So \(a_n<2\) for all \(n\).

Increasing (induction). \(a_2>a_1\) since \(\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}>\sqrt2\). If \(a_n>a_{n-1}\), then \(2+a_n>2+a_{n-1}\), and taking square roots, \(a_{n+1}>a_n\). So the sequence is increasing.

Conclusion. By the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem A.5) the sequence converges, say to \(L\). Taking the limit in the recurrence (the limit of \(a_{n+1}\) is also \(L\), and the square root is continuous) gives \(L=\sqrt{2+L}\), so \(L^2-L-2=0\), that is \((L-2)(L+1)=0\). Because \(a_n>0\) for all \(n\), the limit is not \(-1\). Therefore \(L=2\), and by Theorem A.6 this agrees with \(L\le 2\).

Example A.9: A nonincreasing sequence bounded below

Let \(a_1=2\) and \(a_{n+1}=\dfrac12\left(a_n+\dfrac2{a_n}\right)\). Show that \(\{a_n\}\) converges and find its limit.

Terms. \(a_2=\frac12\left(2+1\right)=\frac32\) and \(a_3=\frac12\left(\frac32+\frac43\right)=\frac{17}{12}\).

Bounded below by \(\sqrt2\). For \(a_n>0\),

\[a_{n+1}^2-2=\frac14\left(a_n+\frac2{a_n}\right)^2-2=\frac14\left(a_n-\frac2{a_n}\right)^2\ge0 ,\]

because \(\left(u+v\right)^2-4uv=(u-v)^2\) with \(u=a_n\), \(v=2/a_n\) and \(uv=2\). So \(a_{n+1}\ge\sqrt2\) for every \(n\), and \(a_1=2>\sqrt2\) too. All terms are positive, so the argument applies at every step.

Nonincreasing. Since \(a_n\ge\sqrt2\) we have \(a_n^2\ge2\), so \(\frac2{a_n}\le a_n\) and

\[a_{n+1}-a_n=\frac12\left(\frac2{a_n}-a_n\right)\le0 .\]

Conclusion. By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, part (b), the sequence converges to some \(L\ge\sqrt2\). Taking limits in the recurrence gives \(L=\frac12\left(L+\frac2L\right)\), so \(2L=L+\frac2L\), \(L=\frac2L\), \(L^2=2\). Since \(L\ge\sqrt2>0\), \(L=\sqrt2\). (This is Newton’s method for \(\sqrt2\).)

items.title: Appendix B. Limit Facts for Sequences
items.text:
Throughout, “for large \(n\)” means “for every \(n\) greater than some integer \(N\)”. We use the \(\varepsilon\)–\(N\) definition (Definition A.2) and the triangle inequality \(\abs{u+v}\le\abs u+\abs v\).

Theorem B.1: Uniqueness of limits

A sequence has at most one limit.

Proof. Suppose \(a_n o L\) and \(a_n o L'\) with \(L e L'\). Let \(\varepsilon= rac12\abs{L-L'}>0\). There are integers \(N_1,N_2\) with \(\abs{a_n-L}<\varepsilon\) for \(n>N_1\) and \(\abs{a_n-L'}<\varepsilon\) for \(n>N_2\). For \(n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}\),

\[\abs{L-L'}\le\abs{L-a_n}+\abs{a_n-L'}<2\varepsilon=\abs{L-L'},\]

a contradiction. So \(L=L'\). ◻ ∎

Theorem B.2: Convergent sequences are bounded

If \(\{a_n\}\) converges, then there is a number \(K\) with \(\abs{a_n}\le K\) for every \(n\).

Proof. Let \(a_n o L\). Taking \(\varepsilon=1\), there is \(N\) with \(\abs{a_n-L}<1\) for \(n>N\), so \(\abs{a_n}\le\abs L+1\) for \(n>N\). Take \(K=\max\{\abs{a_1},\dots,\abs{a_N},\abs L+1\}\). ◻ ∎

Theorem B.3: Tails and absolute values

(a) If \(a_n=b_n\) for all \(n>M\) (for some \(M\)), then \(\{a_n\}\) converges if and only if \(\{b_n\}\) converges, and then the limits are equal. Likewise \(a_n o L\) if and only if \(a_{n+p} o L\) for any fixed integer \(p\ge0\).

(b) \(a_n o0\) if and only if \(\abs{a_n} o0\).

Proof. (a) Let \(b_n o L\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). There is \(N\) with \(\abs{b_n-L}<\varepsilon\) for \(n>N\). Then for \(n>\max\{N,M\}\) we have \(a_n=b_n\), so \(\abs{a_n-L}<\varepsilon\). The converse is the same with the roles exchanged. The shifted sequence \(a_{n+p}\) agrees, after the index change \(m=n+p\), with the terms \(a_m\), \(m>N+p\), so the same \(N\) works with \(N+p\) replaced by \(N\).

(b) The statements \(\abs{a_n-0}<\varepsilon\) and \(\abs{\,\abs{a_n}-0\,}<\varepsilon\) are the same inequality. ◻ ∎

Theorem B.4: Limit laws for sequences

Let \(a_n o A\) and \(b_n o B\), and let \(c\) be a constant. Then

(1) \(a_n\pm b_n o A\pm B\);

(2) \(ca_n o cA\);

(3) \(a_nb_n o AB\);

(4) \(a_n/b_n o A/B\), provided \(B e0\).

Proof. (1) Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N_1,N_2\) with \(\abs{a_n-A}<\varepsilon/2\) for \(n>N_1\) and \(\abs{b_n-B}<\varepsilon/2\) for \(n>N_2\). For \(n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}\),

\[\abs{(a_n\pm b_n)-(A\pm B)}\le\abs{a_n-A}+\abs{b_n-B}<\varepsilon .\]

(2) If \(c=0\) the claim is trivial. Otherwise choose \(N\) with \(\abs{a_n-A}<\varepsilon/\abs c\) for \(n>N\); then \(\abs{ca_n-cA}=\abs c\,\abs{a_n-A}<\varepsilon\).

(3) By Theorem B.2 there is \(K>0\) with \(\abs{a_n}\le K\) for all \(n\). Write

\[a_nb_n-AB=a_n(b_n-B)+B(a_n-A),\]

so \(\abs{a_nb_n-AB}\le K\abs{b_n-B}+\abs B\,\abs{a_n-A}\). Choose \(N_1\) with \(\abs{b_n-B}< rac{\varepsilon}{2K}\) for \(n>N_1\) and \(N_2\) with \(\abs{a_n-A}< rac{\varepsilon}{2(\abs B+1)}\) for \(n>N_2\). For \(n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}\) the right side is less than \( rac\varepsilon2+ rac\varepsilon2=\varepsilon\) (using \(\abs B<\abs B+1\)).

(4) First we show \(1/b_n o1/B\). Since \(B e0\), take \(\varepsilon_0=\abs B/2\): there is \(N_0\) with \(\abs{b_n-B}<\abs B/2\) for \(n>N_0\), hence \(\abs{b_n}>\abs B/2\) (so \(b_n e0\)) for \(n>N_0\). For such \(n\),

\[\left| rac1{b_n}- rac1B ight|= rac{\abs{B-b_n}}{\abs{b_n}\,\abs B}< rac{2}{\abs B^{\,2}}\,\abs{b_n-B}.\]

Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N\ge N_0\) with \(\abs{b_n-B}< rac{\varepsilon\abs B^{\,2}}2\) for \(n>N\); then the left side is less than \(\varepsilon\). Now \(a_n/b_n=a_n\cdot(1/b_n) o A\cdot(1/B)\) by part (3). ◻ ∎

Theorem B.5: Squeeze Theorem for sequences

Suppose \(a_n\le b_n\le c_n\) for every \(n\) greater than some index \(M\). If \(a_n o L\) and \(c_n o L\), then \(b_n o L\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N_1\) with \(\abs{a_n-L}<\varepsilon\) for \(n>N_1\), and \(N_2\) with \(\abs{c_n-L}<\varepsilon\) for \(n>N_2\). For \(n>\max\{M,N_1,N_2\}\),

\[L-\varepsilon<a_n\le b_n\le c_n<L+\varepsilon,\]

so \(\abs{b_n-L}<\varepsilon\). ◻ ∎

Theorem B.6: Limits of \(f(a_n)\) and of \(f(n)\)

(a) If \(a_n o L\) and \(f\) is defined at every \(a_n\) and is continuous at \(L\), then \(f(a_n) o f(L)\).

(b) If \(f(n)=a_n\) for every positive integer \(n\) and \(\lim_{x o\infty}f(x)=L\), where \(L\) is a real number, \(\infty\) or \(-\infty\), then \(\lim_{n o\infty}a_n=L\).

Proof. (a) Let \(\varepsilon>0\). By continuity of \(f\) at \(L\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that \(\abs{f(y)-f(L)}<\varepsilon\) whenever \(\abs{y-L}<\delta\). Since \(a_n o L\) there is \(N\) with \(\abs{a_n-L}<\delta\) for \(n>N\). For those \(n\) we get \(\abs{f(a_n)-f(L)}<\varepsilon\).

(b) Suppose first that \(L\) is a real number and let \(\varepsilon>0\). Because \(f(x) o L\) as \(x o\infty\), there is a number \(X\) with \(\abs{f(x)-L}<\varepsilon\) for all \(x>X\). Let \(N\) be an integer with \(N\ge X\). For every \(n>N\) we have \(n>X\), so \(\abs{a_n-L}=\abs{f(n)-L}<\varepsilon\). If \(L=\infty\) and \(K\) is any number, there is \(X\) with \(f(x)>K\) for \(x>X\), and again \(N\ge X\) gives \(a_n=f(n)>K\) for \(n>N\). The case \(L=-\infty\) is the same. ◻ ∎

The converse of part (b) is false: if \(a_n=\cos(2\pi n)\) then \(a_n o1\), but \(\lim_{x o\infty}\cos(2\pi x)\) does not exist.

Example B.7: Finding \(N\) from \(\varepsilon\)

Prove that \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty} rac{2n+1}{n+3}=2\), and find an \(N\) that works for \(\varepsilon=0.001\).

Plan. We must make \(\abs{a_n-2}\) small, so first simplify \(\abs{a_n-2}\) to something we can solve for \(n\).

Solution. For \(n\ge1\),

\[\left| rac{2n+1}{n+3}-2 ight|=\left| rac{2n+1-2n-6}{n+3} ight|= rac{5}{n+3}.\]

Now \( rac5{n+3}<\varepsilon\) exactly when \(n+3> rac5\varepsilon\), that is, when \(n> rac5\varepsilon-3\). So given any \(\varepsilon>0\), any integer \(N\ge rac5\varepsilon-3\) works: for every \(n>N\) we get \(n+3> rac5\varepsilon\) and so \(\abs{a_n-2}<\varepsilon\). That proves the limit is \(2\).

For \(\varepsilon=0.001\): \( rac5\varepsilon-3=4997\), so \(N=4997\) works. Check at the first index covered, \(n=4998\): \( rac{5}{5001}<0.001\).

Example B.8: A Squeeze Theorem argument

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty} rac{n\sin n}{n^2+1}\).

Solution. The numerator oscillates, so the limit laws do not apply directly (they need \(\lim\sin n\) to exist, and it does not). Instead bound the terms. Since \(-1\le\sin n\le1\) and \(n^2+1>0\),

\[- rac{n}{n^2+1}\le rac{n\sin n}{n^2+1}\le rac{n}{n^2+1}.\]

Both outer sequences tend to \(0\) because

\[\lim_{n o\infty} rac{n}{n^2+1}=\lim_{n o\infty} rac{1/n}{1+1/n^2}= rac{0}{1+0}=0\]

by the limit laws (Theorem B.4). By the Squeeze Theorem (Theorem B.5), the limit is \(0\).

Example B.9: Proving that a sequence diverges

Prove directly from the definition that \(a_n=(-1)^n\) diverges.

Plan. If the sequence had a limit \(L\), then eventually all terms would be within a small distance of \(L\), including two consecutive terms. But consecutive terms are \(2\) apart, so they cannot both be close to one number.

Proof. Suppose \(a_n o L\). Take \(\varepsilon=1\). There is \(N\) with \(\abs{a_n-L}<1\) for all \(n>N\). Pick any \(n>N\); then \(n\) and \(n+1\) are both greater than \(N\), and

\[2=\abs{a_n-a_{n+1}}=\abs{(a_n-L)+(L-a_{n+1})}\le\abs{a_n-L}+\abs{L-a_{n+1}}<1+1=2 .\]

This says \(2<2\), which is impossible. Hence no limit exists. (The same argument with \(\varepsilon\) smaller than half the gap shows that any sequence whose terms keep jumping between two different values diverges.)

Example B.10: A limit of the form \(f(a_n)\)

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n o\infty}\cos\!\left( rac{\pi n}{2n+1} ight)\).

Solution. Let \(a_n=\dfrac{n}{2n+1}\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(n\), \(a_n=\dfrac{1}{2+1/n} o\dfrac12\) by the limit laws. The function \(f(y)=\cos(\pi y)\) is continuous at every number, in particular at \( rac12\). By Theorem B.6(a),

\[\cos(\pi a_n) o\cos\!\left( rac\pi2 ight)=0 .\]
